title: A Simple Daily Observation and Grow Log

content.overview: Home growers improve faster when they record a few consistent observations rather than trying to remember everything. A short log turns environmental and plant changes into trends you can compare.

vocabulary.definition: A normal reference condition used to judge later changes.
A directional pattern across repeated observations.
To inspect plants systematically for health, pest or disease changes.

sections.title: Record the same core variables
sections.body: Date, stage, temperature/RH, irrigation, major plant changes and pest/disease observations are enough to make many home problems easier to interpret.

sections.title: Look under and inside the canopy
sections.body: Pests and humidity problems can begin where casual top-down observation misses them.

sections.title: Photos work best with context
sections.body: Repeat photos from similar positions and label them with date and plant ID so visual change is comparable.

workedExamples: A three-day trend of slower dryback is more informative than saying the pot feels wet today.
A pest photo without plant/location/date information is less useful than a smaller image tied to a consistent scout record.
commonMistakes: Logging only when plants look bad.
content.practicalApplication: Use a daily five-minute log and a longer weekly inspection. Keep the format simple enough that you will actually maintain it.
content.summary: Consistent small observations build the evidence needed for better home-grow decisions.
